Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Tech companies think most senior developers who fail interviews lack problem-solving skills. About 99% of developers are in this category. Why don't these incompetent developers focus on improving their skills instead of blaming the entire system?
Answer: I disagree with several parts of your problem, so let me break it down. Tech companies think most senior developers who fail interviews lack problem-solving skills. No, they don’t. Big tech companies are well aware that their interview processes filter out many strong candidates. However, they enjoy the luxury of having so many candidates to choose from that they can enforce extremely demanding interview processes and still meet their recruitment targets. About 99% of developers are in this category. Perhaps if you count everyone who considers themselves a developer that would be the case. But among strongly qualified developers, I think the percentage who fails outright on the coding problems is much lower. Why don't these incompetent developers focus on improving their skills instead of blaming the entire system? First of all, just because someone fails big tech interview problems doesn't mean they're incompetent. These problems typically have very little to do with the actual job of being a developer. Among those who would fail, I find that most simply don't care. They can find great jobs elsewhere, so why bother studying undergraduate-level computer science again just for the possibility that some big corporation might hire them?

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: What do you think about Magnus Carlsen resigning after 2 moves against Hans Niemann?
Answer: Magnus is clearly making a statement. That he doesn't want to play with cheaters. The moment Magnus resigned. Niemann is a proven cheater in online tournaments. Even after getting caught, he has been a repeat offender over several years. You could say “it's only online”, but this downplays the severity of his actions too much. Some of the tournaments he cheated in had significant prize money. What he has been doing is undermining the game of chess in a bad way. Even worse, it looks quite likely that Niemann cheated in over-the -board tournaments to achieve his final Grandmaster norm and secure the GM title. Analysis has surfaced that seems to show this convincingly. If true, this means he obtained the title illegitimately, and has gotten away with it (so far). There should be some form of repercussions. On the other hand, I don't think Magnus is handling this in the most elegant way. Resigning after one move with no explanation is just passive-aggressive. It seems that Niemann got in Magnus’ head with his trash-talk, and now Magnus has seen red. What he should have done in my opinion is to come right out and say it. “Niemann is a cheater and I don't want to play with him”. I believe he would have garnered more respect from the chess community that way. This is the second top-level tournament that's being disrupted by this unresolved drama. The chess world needs some form of resolution. Even if Niemann has cheated several times, he is still young, and he should get a chance to redeem himself. All this drama can be very damaging to him, both as a chess player and as a human being. He deserves a fair trial, not to be pilloried.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Who is earning more, an engineering manager or a solution architect?
Answer: Whoever has the higher market(*) value and/or higher willingness to move around to cash in on that market value earns more. * Market value, here meaning the minimum amount that employers in the geographical region think they have to pay to sign that person with a decent likelihood that they'll stay for a few years.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: Will companies use an AI API like chatgpt? I don't mean that they will take over the machine learning jobs, but I do mean that companies will use the API instead of bringing in machine learning engineers?
Answer: Absolutely. At my company (sklls.ai), we develop conversational AI for call centers. In the past, we trained our own intent recognition models based on recurrent neural networks such as LSTMs, and I had highly-paid machine learning engineers helping me with that. The challenge there, as has always been the main challenge in my career as a machine learning engineer, is to collect enough data. We had tens of thousands of samples and a good model architecture, but it just wasn’t enough for a data-hungry deep neural network. In fact, very simple similarity-matching algorithms like the Sørensen-Dice coefficient would routinely outperform our deep learning models. As an early-stage startup, it takes time to gain a large enough user base to collect the volume of data needed for high performance. In October 2022, when the GPT-3.5 version of InstructGPT was launched, we started using this model through OpenAI’s Completions API as an integral part of our core AI. This revolutionized the conversations we could provide through our platform. The main win there is that the GPT models are pretrained and don’t need training data. The GPT-3 paper was literally called Large Language Models are Few-Shot Learners. By complementing our existing intent-based solution with GPT-3.5 the AI became much more robust. It could give reasonable answers even when the users went outside the scope of our intents. Last month, when the ChatGPT API was launched, we upgraded to that. The feedback from users is amazing. This model knocks it out of the park even when compared to GPT-3.5 model we were using up until now. This doesn’t mean it will replace our machine learning efforts entirely. We are still training in-house models for speech recognition, speech synthesis and intent recognition. But it definitely helps to magnify the results provided by our AI team. I think we’ll quickly see a new breed of AI engineers that don’t necessarily have the theoretical foundation of a data scientist. You don’t need that to use the ChatGPT API.

Name: Håkon Hapnes Strand
Question: As a software engineering manager, how do you balance tech debt vs feature development work for your team?
Answer: Most software engineering managers are middle managers. They're in that famous squeeze between their team and higher-level management. The squeeze is primarily a people problem and not so much a tech problem. You have to answer to sales who wants to please their prospects to meet quotas. Then you have executive management who wants to show off innovation when presenting the company outward. And finally you have your engineers, who usually have the product's best interests at heart, but are also often naive to the harsh realities of running a business. Balancing all of that is an impossible task, so you try to be practical and give a little in every direction to keep everyone somewhat pleased. A well-run tech company will have a VP of Engineering that shields their engineering managers from outside pressures so that the engineering managers in turn can shield their engineers and deliver the best possible product.
